introduction_markdown: Multiple choice question paper (English Language 1, June 2020, Advanced Level, subject code 0730). Time allowed: one and a half hours. Answer ALL 50 questions; all questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D: choose the one that best answers the question and mark only one answer for each question. Do all rough work in the question booklet. The paper has three sections: A reading comprehension (16 marks, questions 1-16, one long passage), B grammar (22 marks, questions 17-38) and C vocabulary (12 marks, questions 39-50).
enonce_intro_markdown: **Multiple choice questions** - choose the one best answer, A, B, C or D.
incertitudes: Page de garde vérifiée : « 0730 ENGLISH LANGUAGE 1 », « JUNE 2020 », « ADVANCED LEVEL », « MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTION PAPER », une heure et demie, 50 questions à points égaux. Sections imprimées : A Reading comprehension (16 Marks, questions 1-16), B Grammar (22 Marks, questions 17-38), C Vocabulary (12 Marks, questions 39-50). Aucune règle de choix : tout est obligatoire.
Aucun corrigé officiel : toutes les clés sont établies par la règle de langue ou par le passage, en insérant chaque option dans la phrase.

Le passage de lecture est recopié en entier ; les numéros de ligne imprimés (5, 10, ..., 80) sont repris entre crochets à la fin de la ligne imprimée. Les paragraphes sont comptés par saut de ligne (question 8 : le paragraphe 6 commence par « But for the moment » ; question 12 : le paragraphe 8 commence par « Frequent droughts »). Le texte imprimé dit « the group that helped Wilson » sans présenter Wilson (texte adapté), gardé tel quel.
Les mots soulignés dans le sujet imprimé (questions 38, 45 à 50) sont rendus en gras, faute de souligné fiable en Markdown.

Consignes imprimées qui se recouvrent : « For questions 39 - 45 » (complétion) puis « For questions 45-50 » (mots soulignés) ; la question 45 est bien une question de mots soulignés (sens de licensed). La section C porte donc la consigne 39-45 sur la question 39 et la consigne 45-50 sur la question 45.

Clés retenues mais discutables (option concurrente entre parenthèses) : question 2 : A (B, C défendables seulement si « incredible » est lu comme « difficile à croire ») ; question 8 : B (A, devastate, est un effet évoqué ailleurs dans le passage) ; question 9 : A (D, denial, est aussi un obstacle cité au début) ; question 14 : B (D, transportation, est l'autre moitié du même constat d'isolement) ; question 16 : B (C, dissatisfaction, pour les critiques du gouvernement) ; question 24 : C (D would you est un tag de politesse, B can you moins courant) ; question 39 : C runny (D running est courant à l'oral) ; question 15 : C (B, la difficulté du combat, est un thème secondaire).

Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 4, 10, 23, 34, 46, 47. Q4 : misappropriation (A) ou corruption (B). Q10 : acronym (B) ou abbreviation (A). Q23 : with whom (B, collocation standard) ou in whom (A, citation biblique). Q34 : backshift (A) ou présent conservé pour une vérité permanente (C). Q46 : cheat on each other (A) ou unfaithful to each other (D), quasi-synonymes. Q47 : betrayed him (B) ou revealed him (A).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section A - Reading comprehension (16 marks).** *Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions below it.*

**Passage for questions 1 to 16** (the numbers in square brackets are the line numbers printed in the paper, at the end of the printed line)

Africa's response to AIDS is often depicted to be as dysfunctional as its economy, just another example of what some AIDS workers call "Afro-pessimism" - only bad news coming out of Africa. It is true that just a handful of African governments have mobilized a response remotely commensurate with the magnitude of the epidemic, which has already slashed life expectancy by as much as 20 years in some countries. AIDS stigma has also made many ordinary people shy away [5] from dealing with the epidemic. "I have found the most unacceptable denial and apathy in Africa," says Elhadji Sy, who heads the southern and eastern African team for UNIAIDS. "But on the other hand, the most incredible responses to HIV have been developed here. We live in this contradiction of extremes."

Nowhere are these extremes more pronounced than in Zimbabwe, the former Rhodesia, which [10] whites ruled until 1980. When it finally gained independence, Zimbabwe was the South Africa of its day - relatively prosperous, with no foreign debt, and a currency stronger than the U.S. dollar. Now, the economy is in free-fall, and a quarter of adults in the prime of life, aged 15 to 49, are infected with HIV. The virus is killing more than 65,000 people a year.

Yet the director of Zimbabwe's National AIDS Coordination Programme, Everisto Marova, says [15] that government spending on AIDS prevention has, in real terms, "certainly not increased and probably declined" over the last five years. Last month, the government announced a special AIDS tax, but even AIDS workers criticized the idea because the government provided no plans on how it would spend the money. Corruption and mismanagement are rife in Zimbabwe, and previous special levies have disappeared with no accounting. [20]

Yet below the radar of government, in individual communities there are astonishingly vigorous responses to AIDS. "In every province we have member organizations," says Thembeni Mahlangu, director of the Zimbabwe AIDS Network. "They were often started by a church or NGO [nongovernmental organization] and sometimes just by individuals." For example, Auxilia Chimusoro founded Zimbabwe's first AIDS support group, and then tirelessly travelled the country [25] launching more. By the time she died in 1998, Chimusoro had started more than 50 support groups, most in poor rural communities. In the capital, Harare, the Musasa Project works with battered women, helping them break free of partners who often force them to have sex almost always without a condom. IGAC, the group that helped Wilson, specializes in home-based care and orphan [30] support and it has recently launched a youth prevention campaign. The leadership of most AIDS programmes "is composed of professionals," says Lucia Malemane, a nurse with Zimbabwe's Matabeleland AIDS Council, who taught Insiza about AIDS. "But with IGAC, it's just ordinary peasant farmers."

Heroic as these efforts may be, they are tinged with poignancy - and not just because the government, which could knit these isolated efforts into a powerful national response, has shirked [35] its duty. Most community programmes lack any but the most basic medicines. Certainly, they cannot afford the expensive regimens that have reduced the AIDS death rate in wealthy countries. Without effective drugs, home-based care can seem like little more than home-based death. With the disease mowing down so many people, and with poverty making volunteering so burdensome, it remains to be seen whether such homespun efforts can endure for the decades that may well pass [40] before an AIDS vaccine is developed.

But for the moment, thousands of ordinary Africans are defying all odds to care for their sick, raise their orphans, and try to slow the virus's spread. If governments finally mobilize against this disease, they will find some of the best and most energetic AIDS strategies right under their noses. And they might find something else. Traditionally, Africans relied on extended families and tight [45] communities to weather adversity, but even before AIDS, colonialism, urbanization, and social atomization had weakened the sinews of African society. The epidemic threatens to snap them, but it could also have the opposite effect. "AIDS is horrible, but in times of great stress, societies can either fall apart or come together," says Alan Whiteside, who studies the demographic impact of AIDS at South Africa's University of Natal. Noting how the American gay community built [50] powerful institutions and a stronger culture, he says that "IGAC, with a little help, could be an example of building civil society in Africa."

There are few places where the difficulties of responding to AIDS are more daunting than here in Insiza, a flat, dry district of southern Zimbabwe. Villagers here are so poor that most don't bury their dead in coffins, but merely wrap them in blankets. At one funeral, near the start of [55] Zimbabwe's winter, the grieving family was so destitute that, after lowering the body into the grave, they started removing the blanket from the corpse so their children wouldn't go cold. Stricken with pity and horror, IGAC's coordinator, Japhet Gwebu gave the family a blanket. Only about half of Insiza's population can read and write, and what schools there are, often lack even furniture, forcing students to work on the floor. The district hospital is supposed to have five [60] doctors, but on a recent visit, it had only one, and the operating theatre was closed because the hospital had run out of anaesthetics. Nurses are also in short supply - but not patients, who have poured in over and above capacity.

Frequent droughts cause starvation. The 1992 drought killed most of the cattle, which means that even though the rains were good this year, many prime fields lay untilled because there are no [65] beasts of burden to pull the plough. Nobody, of course, has tractors or automobiles. How many residents have electricity or running water? Back in the late 1980s, when a new disease began causing people to waste into skin-shrouded skeletons, most people in Insiza believed the affliction was caused by witchcraft. Only in 1994 did they learn the medical facts, and immediately a group of elders decided they needed to do something to care for the droves of sick people and the swelling [70] number of orphans, but how to organize the villages remained the burning issue.

Homesteads are scattered far apart, yet throughout the district's 7,500 square kilometres - an area larger than Delaware - there is only one paved road. Nobody has telephones. Isaiah Ndlovu, one of IGAC's founders and most active leaders, has never even heard of e-mail, but he sometimes sends messages by relay, villagers passing on his communiqué so that by the end of the day it has [75] travelled across the vast farmland to its intended recipient - if someone hasn't misunderstood the message or forgotten it completely. So to mobilize his community, Ndlovu must visit homesteads one by one, and that's how he keeps the programme going, checking in on the volunteers and the dying people they're caring for.

It is often said that Africans are passive in the face of death and suffering, that life is cheap here. [80] The truth is that life is hard. People are so poor that even when they give a large proportion of their income, as most IGAC volunteers do, the total amounts to only a small sum - so small that even bare-bones efforts are hard to launch and maintain. Groups like IGAC are "isolated and scattered blossoms," as Kaleeba puts it, adding, "I wish this blossom could be turned into a flower garden."

*Adapted from "The Village Voice" by Jason Schartzberg - a Research intern; November 23, 1999.*

**Questions 1 to 16** *(choose the best answer for each question from the alternatives A, B, C or D)*

1. When the writer says, "Africa's response to AIDS has been dysfunctional...," it suggests that it has \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Dysfunctional" means not working as it should. A response that is dysfunctional is one that has produced no results, which is what "not yielded fruits" says. "Laudable" and "appropriate" are favourable judgements and contradict the word. "A sham" means a pretence or fake, which is not the same as a failure to work. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 2. The writer thinks that there is a "contradiction of extremes" as far as AIDS is concerned because there is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Elhadji Sy sets the "most unacceptable denial and apathy" (lines 6-7) against "the most incredible responses to HIV" (lines 7-8), then calls this "this contradiction of extremes". The two extremes are therefore refusal to face the disease and a remarkable ("incredible" in the sense of astonishing, admirable) readiness to respond to it. Option A states exactly this pair, denial and acceptance. B and C add "total", which the passage does not say, and turn "incredible" into "believable" or "unbelievable", which misreads a positive word. D has no denial, so no contradiction. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: total denial of and a believable response to AIDS
total denial of and an unbelievable response to AIDS
total acceptance and response to AIDS

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 3. In paragraph 2, the comparison between Zimbabwe and South Africa is in terms of their \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Paragraph 2 says Zimbabwe "was the South Africa of its day - relatively prosperous, with no foreign debt, and a currency stronger than the U.S. dollar". Prosperity, absence of debt and a strong currency are all aspects of economic strength. Currency alone is only one detail inside the comparison, so B is too narrow. Apartheid and AIDS statistics are not compared. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 4. The institution of the special AIDS tax was greatly criticized due to fear of \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) misappropriation   B) corruption   C) accountability   D) tax evasion
questions.corrige_markdown:
Lines 17-20 give the reason: AIDS workers criticized the tax "because the government provided no plans on how it would spend the money", and "previous special levies have disappeared with no accounting". The fear was that the money would be diverted or misused, which is misappropriation. Corruption (B) is the background that makes the fear reasonable ("Corruption and mismanagement are rife") and is close in meaning, so A and B overlap. Accountability (C) is what is lacking, not what is feared. Tax evasion (D) concerns taxpayers, not the government. The best fit is A, but B can be defended.

**Intended answer: A (misappropriation).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 5. According to the text, the target groups for AIDS support programmes are \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The programmes named in paragraph 4 work with "battered women" who are forced into unprotected sex (the Musasa Project) and with "orphan support" (IGAC). Farmers are the people who run IGAC ("just ordinary peasant farmers"), not the people it helps, so A, C and D are wrong. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 6. The expression, "the government ... has shirked its duty." (line 34-36) means \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: To shirk a duty is to avoid it or neglect it. The government "could knit these isolated efforts into a powerful national response" but has not done so, so it has abandoned its responsibility. "Taken" and "recognized" are the opposite. "Transferred" suggests handing the duty to someone else, which the passage does not say. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 7. In the statement, "Africans relied on extended families and tight communities to weather adversity...," (lines 45-46) 'to weather adversity' is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: To weather a storm is to come safely through it. Here the verb is applied, not to a real storm, but to hardship ("adversity"): one thing is described in terms of another without "like" or "as". That is a metaphor. There is no contrast between meaning and what is said (irony, sarcasm) and adversity is not given human qualities (personification). **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - figures of speech

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 8. In paragraph 6, the most significant effects of AIDS is seen in its ability to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Paragraph 6 ("But for the moment, thousands of ordinary Africans ...") says the epidemic "threatens to snap" the weakened social fabric "but it could also have the opposite effect": "in times of great stress, societies can either fall apart or come together", and groups like IGAC show "building civil society". The effect the paragraph stresses as significant is therefore the power to bring people together. Devastating, impoverishing and isolating are effects of AIDS mentioned elsewhere, or not at all, but they are not what this paragraph develops. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 9. One major obstacle to the fight against the AIDS pandemic in Africa is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Poverty runs through the whole passage: it makes volunteering "so burdensome" (line 39), leaves villagers unable to buy coffins, and means that even large proportions of income "amount to only a small sum" so that "bare-bones efforts are hard to launch and maintain" (lines 81-83). Drought is mentioned but only as a local hardship, illiteracy is mentioned once (half the population can read and write), and denial appears only in the first paragraph and is balanced by the vigorous responses. The most repeated obstacle is poverty. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
(Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 10. IGAC as used in the passage is an example of the use of \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) abbreviation   B) acronym   C) mnemonic   D) capitalization
questions.corrige_markdown:
IGAC is a name made from initial letters, so it is a shortened form of a longer name. An acronym is a word formed from the initial letters of a name; in school usage the term covers such initial-letter names, and this is the usual answer. "Abbreviation" is the broader term and is also true. A mnemonic is a memory aid and capitalization is just the use of capital letters. A and B therefore overlap, and the choice depends on how strictly "acronym" is taken.

**Intended answer: B (acronym).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 11. The people of Insiza demonstrate a nonchalant attitude towards the dead because of \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: Lines 54-58: the villagers are so poor that they bury their dead in blankets, and one family even took the blanket back from the corpse so their children would not be cold. The writer explains the attitude in the last paragraph: "The truth is that life is hard." The cause is a difficult way of life. Pride and a lavish life-style do not fit people in destitution, and "horrible" is an exaggeration of what the text says. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 12. In paragraph 8, the expression, "... a new disease began causing people to waste into skin-shrouded skeletons ..." is the writer's way of saying that \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Waste" here means to lose flesh gradually, and "skin-shrouded skeletons" describes bodies in which the bones show beneath the skin. The idea is extreme thinness caused by sickness, that is, emaciation due to illness (D). A is too general, B takes "waste" in the wrong sense (to squander), and C leaves out the cause. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context
A Level English - figures of speech

choix.texte: the people emaciated due to illness

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 13. In the statement, "... only in 1994 did they learn the medical facts..." (line 69), 'medical' is used as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Medical" comes before the noun "facts" and describes it (facts about medicine), so it is an adjective. The noun is "medicine" and the adverb is "medically". **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 14. The most outstanding impediment to the realization of IGAC's project is the \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: In paragraph 9 the writer shows how scattered the homesteads are: "Nobody has telephones", Ndlovu "has never even heard of e-mail", and messages must travel "by relay", with the risk that the message is "misunderstood" or "forgotten". Because there is no way to reach people quickly, he has to visit homesteads "one by one" to mobilize them. The obstacle that dominates the paragraph is the lack of communication facilities. Transport is also lacking (one paved road, no vehicles), but it is mentioned as part of the same picture of isolation. People are willing to cooperate (A is wrong). **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: lack of cooperation among the people

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 15. The writer's intention in this passage is to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The writer begins by challenging "Afro-pessimism", spends the middle of the passage on grassroots groups such as the Zimbabwe AIDS Network, the Musasa Project and IGAC, and ends with IGAC as an example of civil society. The government's failure and the difficulties are used as a background that makes these efforts look more remarkable. The main intention is to salute the efforts of these organizations. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

choix.texte: expose African governments' lack of response to AIDS
show how difficult it is to fight AIDS in Africa
salute the efforts made by some organizations to fight AIDS in Africa
show the effects of AIDS on Africa

questions.enonce_markdown: (Passage for questions 1 to 16 above) 16. The general tone of the passage is one of \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The passage rejects "Afro-pessimism" in its first lines and speaks of "astonishingly vigorous" responses, ordinary Africans "defying all odds", and societies that can "come together". It does admit sorrow ("tinged with poignancy") and criticises the government, but the overall attitude is hopeful, a cautious optimism. Pessimism is the attitude it argues against, and apathy is something it condemns (line 6). **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - tone and attitude

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section B - Grammar (22 marks).** Choose the alternative A, B, C or D that best completes each sentence below.

17. "My daughter, can you take a rest now? \_\_\_\_\_\_ since morning."
questions.corrige_markdown: The action began in the morning and is still going on now ("can you take a rest now?"), so the present perfect continuous is needed: "You have been reading since morning." "Since" with a point in time goes with a perfect tense, not with the simple present or past. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 18. My brother called to congratulate me \_\_\_\_\_\_ my success at the GCE Examination.
questions.corrige_markdown: The verb "congratulate" takes "on" before the achievement: congratulate someone on something. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 19. "The decision has been taken so, \_\_\_\_\_\_ hard you try, things aren't going to change in your favour," the manager told the employee.
questions.corrige_markdown: "However" followed by an adjective or adverb means "no matter how": "however hard you try". "If" and "although" cannot be placed before "hard" in this way, and "nevertheless" is a linking adverb that joins sentences, not a word that introduces a clause. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 20. If I had known you were attending the wedding, I \_\_\_\_\_\_ a hotel room for you.
questions.corrige_markdown: "If I had known" is a past unreal condition (third conditional), so the main clause takes "would have" + past participle: "I would have reserved a hotel room for you." "Would reserve" is a second conditional form and "will have reserved" is a future perfect. "Should have reserved" expresses a missed duty, not a result of the condition. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 21. The criminals were very smart. They could \_\_\_\_\_\_ their fate and pre-empt it by escaping.
questions.corrige_markdown: The fixed expression is "only too clearly", meaning "very clearly", placed after the verb: "They could see only too clearly their fate." The adverbs stay together after "see". In A, C and D the words are scattered and the meaning is lost. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: 22. All sports lovers in the country \_\_\_\_\_\_ the new coach of the Indomitable Lions to win the next tournament.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Look up to" someone means to respect them and to count on them. The sports lovers are counting on the coach to win. "Look up for" and "look up on" are not phrasal verbs with this sense, and "look up at" means to raise one's eyes towards something. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
23. This is my son \_\_\_\_\_\_ I am well pleased.

*Options as printed:* A) in whom   B) with whom   C) in who   D) with who
questions.corrige_markdown:
The adjective "pleased" takes the preposition "with" (to be pleased with someone), and in a relative clause the preposition comes before "whom": "This is my son with whom I am well pleased." "Who" cannot follow a preposition, so C and D are ruled out. Option A reproduces the scriptural phrase "in whom I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17), which is a fixed quotation and may be the one the setter had in mind; as ordinary grammar, however, "pleased with" is the standard collocation. Because A and B are both defensible and the Board's key is not known, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (with whom).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: 24. Don't be stupid enough to confront him, \_\_\_\_\_\_?
questions.corrige_markdown: After an imperative, including a negative one, the usual question tag is "will you?": "Don't be stupid enough to confront him, will you?" "Do you" would be used after a negative statement with a verb in the simple present, not after an imperative. "Would you" is a politer request tag and "can you" asks about ability, so they are less standard. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
25. "Will you marry me, Mary?" I asked.
I asked Mary if \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: In reported speech the reporting verb is in the past ("asked"), so "will" changes to "would", and the question becomes a clause with "if" in statement order: "if she would marry me". D changes the meaning ("would like to" is not in the original), and B and C keep "will". **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: she will like to marry me
she would like to marry me

questions.enonce_markdown: 26. \_\_\_\_\_\_ when trouble started.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Hardly" at the beginning of a sentence is followed by inversion (auxiliary before subject) and by the past perfect for the first action: "Hardly had I arrived when trouble started." The other options use the wrong tense or no inversion. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 27. We tried hard, and in the end, we were able to make Herman \_\_\_\_\_\_ his car for an hour.
questions.corrige_markdown: After "make" in the active (make someone do something) the bare infinitive is used, without "to": "make Herman lend his car". (The "to" appears only in the passive: "Herman was made to lend...") **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 28. I look forward to \_\_\_\_\_\_ from you soon.
questions.corrige_markdown: In "look forward to", "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund (-ing form): "I look forward to hearing from you soon." **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 29. \_\_\_\_\_\_ of his friends speaks any English.
questions.corrige_markdown: The verb "speaks" is singular, so the subject must be a singular pronoun. "Neither (of)" takes a singular verb, and "any" fits a negative sense (neither of them speaks any English). "Few", "some" and "many" take plural verbs. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 30. \_\_\_\_\_\_ are going to Mawah for dinner.
questions.corrige_markdown: The compound is the subject of "are going", so the subject pronouns are required (not "him" or "me"), and courtesy puts the other person first: "He and I". **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 31. I don't feel well - I think I am going to \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Throw up" is the phrasal verb meaning to vomit, which suits "I don't feel well". "Throw off" means to get rid of, "throw out" to expel or discard, and "throw in" to add. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 32. He fell in love with a \_\_\_\_\_\_ lady.
questions.corrige_markdown: Adjectives follow the order opinion, then size, then age, shape, colour and so on. "Smart" and "beautiful" are opinions and "tall" is size, so both opinions come first and "tall" last: "smart, beautiful, tall". Each of the other options puts "tall" before an opinion adjective. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
33. The Professor asked the graduate, "What have you been doing since you left the university?"
The Professor asked the graduate \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: With a past reporting verb ("asked"), the present perfect continuous ("have been doing") moves back to the past perfect continuous ("had been doing"), and the simple past "left" stays as it is. The question also loses its inversion. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: what he has been doing since he left the university
what he had been doing since he left the university
what he was doing since he left the university
what he has done since he left the university

questions.enonce_markdown:
34. "Cameroon is in Central Africa," Ndongo said.
Ndongo \_\_\_\_\_\_.

*Options as printed:* A) said that Cameroon was in Central Africa   B) says that Cameroon is in Central Africa   C) said that Cameroon is in Central Africa   D) says that Cameroon was in Central Africa
questions.corrige_markdown:
The original sentence has "said", so the reporting verb must stay in the past and B and D are ruled out. With a past reporting verb the usual rule backshifts "is" to "was": "said that Cameroon was in Central Africa" (A). However, the statement is a permanent fact, and English allows the present tense to be kept after a past reporting verb when the fact is still true: "said that Cameroon is in Central Africa" (C). A tests the backshift rule; C is also correct. Because both are defensible and the Board's key is not known, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: A (said that Cameroon was in Central Africa).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
35. She is making a new dress for her sister.
The passive form of this sentence is:
questions.corrige_markdown: The active verb is the present continuous ("is making"), so the passive is "is being made", with the object "a new dress" as the new subject. A is present perfect, B past continuous and D past perfect. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: A new dress has been made for her sister.
A new dress was being made for her sister.
A new dress is being made for her sister.
A new dress had been made for her sister.

questions.enonce_markdown: 36. The proprietor noticed that after a long day of hard work, the workers as well as the foreman, \_\_\_\_\_\_ famished.
questions.corrige_markdown: The subject is "the workers" (plural). The phrase "as well as the foreman" is added information and does not change the number of the verb. The verb is in the past because it depends on "noticed" and describes the state after the day's work: "the workers ... were famished". **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
37. **From the alternatives A, B, C or D, choose the sentence that is correctly punctuated.**

A. John is a good driver, moreover, he is very friendly.
B. John is a good driver; Moreover, he is very friendly.
C. John is a good driver: Moreover he is very friendly.
D. John is a good driver; moreover, he is very friendly.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Moreover" is a conjunctive adverb. Two independent clauses joined by it need a semicolon before it and a comma after it, and "moreover" is not capitalized after a semicolon. A is a comma splice, B wrongly capitalizes "Moreover", and C uses a colon, which introduces an explanation or a list, not an addition. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - spelling and punctuation

choix.texte: John is a good driver, moreover, he is very friendly.
John is a good driver; Moreover, he is very friendly.
John is a good driver: Moreover he is very friendly.
John is a good driver; moreover, he is very friendly.

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For question 38, choose the alternative A, B, C or D that gives the function of the underlined part of the sentence.*

38. He became **a doctor**.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Became" is a linking verb. The noun phrase after it does not receive the action but renames the subject (He = a doctor), so it is a subject complement. A direct object follows a transitive verb, an indirect object receives the direct object, and an adjunct is an optional adverbial. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**Section C - Vocabulary (12 marks).** *For questions 39 - 45, choose the alternative A, B, C or D, that best completes each sentence.*

39. I noticed that the lady was very uncomfortable because of her \_\_\_\_\_\_ nose.
questions.corrige_markdown: A nose that keeps discharging mucus is a "runny nose", the standard adjective in this collocation. "Watery" describes eyes or liquids, and "wetting" is not used of a nose. "Running nose" is heard in everyday speech but "runny" is the standard form. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 40. The \_\_\_\_\_\_ thrilled the \_\_\_\_\_\_ that flocked the hall to watch the play.
questions.corrige_markdown: A play is performed by a cast and watched by an audience, so "the cast thrilled the audience". An orchestra plays music, a staff is a group of employees, a mob is a disorderly crowd, and a team plays a sport. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 41. "Only the Form Four and Lower Sixth students will take part in the \_\_\_\_\_\_," the principal announced.
questions.corrige_markdown: A "march past" is a parade in which a group marches in front of a reviewing officer, usual on national holidays at school. "Match" is a game, and "passed" is the verb form, not the noun. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 42. The congregation watched with admiration as the newly-wedded couple walked down the \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: An aisle is the passage between rows of seats in a church. The other options are homophones or near-homophones: "ail" (to trouble), "ale" (a beer) and "isles" (islands). **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 43. My friend was arrested at the airport because the picture on his passport was \_\_\_\_\_\_ imposed.
questions.corrige_markdown: "Superimposed" means placed over something else, so a picture was fixed over the original one. "Super" is the prefix meaning above or over; "pre-imposed", "overimposed" and "underimposed" are not words. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: 44. Bark is to dog as \_\_\_\_\_\_.
questions.corrige_markdown: The relation is the sound an animal makes. Dogs bark and goats bleat. A cock crows (not a hen), a snake hisses (a cricket chirps), and a horse neighs (a cow lows or moos). **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For questions 45-50, choose the answer from the alternatives A, B, C or D that best explains the underlined words/phrases.*

45. The company is **licensed** to sell biodegradable plastic bags, so they can market them without any harassment.
questions.corrige_markdown: To be licensed to do something is to be given official permission to do it, so "permitted". "Mandated", "ordered" and "obliged" all mean being required to do it, but the sentence says they can sell without harassment, which describes permission. **Answer: A.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
46. A marriage doesn't last long when spouses tend to be **green snakes in green grass**.

*Options as printed:* A) Cheat on each other   B) hypocritical towards each other   C) disrespectful to each other   D) unfaithful to each other
questions.corrige_markdown:
"A snake in the grass" is a treacherous person who hides their betrayal. Spouses who are "green snakes in green grass" hide their deceit from each other, and in a marriage that means infidelity. A ("cheat on each other") and D ("unfaithful to each other") say almost the same thing: A is a verb phrase that would need "to" before it in this sentence, D is an adjective phrase that fits the same "to be ... " pattern. Hypocritical (B) and disrespectful (C) do not describe betrayal. Because A and D are near-synonyms and the Board's key is not known, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: D (unfaithful to each other).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown:
47. On being interrogated at the Immigration Office, the Nigerian said he was a Cameroonian, but his accent **gave him away**.

*Options as printed:* A) revealed him   B) betrayed him   C) proved it   D) concealed it
questions.corrige_markdown:
"To give someone away" means to reveal, usually by accident, who they really are. His accent showed he was not Cameroonian, so it "betrayed him" (exposed the truth against his wish). "Proved it" and "concealed it" do not fit, because "it" has no clear referent and "concealed" is the opposite. "Revealed him" is close in meaning, but "betrayed him" is the idiomatic equivalent of "gave him away", and the two are hard to separate. Because A and B are both defensible, the question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (betrayed him).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: A Level English - idioms and proverbs

questions.enonce_markdown: 48. The witness' arguments instead of helping the defendant only served to **corroborate** the evidence against him.
questions.corrige_markdown: To corroborate is to support or confirm a statement with additional evidence. The witness's arguments, instead of helping, only supported the evidence against the defendant. **Answer: D.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown:
*For questions 49-50, choose the answer from the alternatives A, B, C or D that is opposite in meaning to the underlined words.*

49. The decision of the court was to **convict** the man.
questions.corrige_markdown: To convict is to declare someone guilty. The opposite is to acquit, to declare someone not guilty. "Imprison" is what may follow a conviction and is not its opposite, "bail" is a temporary release before the trial and "judge" is to hear and decide. **Answer: C.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context

questions.enonce_markdown: 50. People who are **extravagant** do not easily make friends.
questions.corrige_markdown: Extravagant means spending far too much money. The opposite is stingy (unwilling to spend). "Spendthrift" is a synonym of extravagant, "selfish" concerns attitude to others and "carefree" means without worry. **Answer: B.**
themes: A Level English - vocabulary in context
